scenes.tts: Meyerhof reached biochemistry by an unlikely road. Bedridden for months by a kidney ailment in his twenties, he read poetry and wrote a doctoral thesis on the psychology of mental illness before deciding that life itself could be written in the language of physical law.

scenes.tts: His 1913 habilitation, "The Energetics of Living Cells," argued that a body is a thermodynamic system holding itself against entropy — and he proved it with frog legs.
scenes.narration: His 1913 habilitation, "The Energetics of Living Cells," argued that a body is a thermodynamic system holding itself against entropy — and he proved it with frog legs.

scenes.tts: Stimulating detached muscle to exhaustion without oxygen, he watched lactic acid pile up; when he readmitted air, only about a quarter of it burned for energy and the rest was rebuilt into glycogen. That recovery loop, the muscle repaying its "oxygen debt," won him a share of the 1922 Nobel Prize.

scenes.tts: The theory was elegant, and he did not cling to it: when his assistant Karl Lohmann isolated ATP in 1929 and muscle was soon shown to contract with no lactic acid at all, Meyerhof retooled his whole laboratory around the new molecule.

scenes.tts: Fleeing France in 1940, found in a Marseille hotel lobby and asked what he needed, he asked not for food but for his notes and his library — and carried both to Pennsylvania.
